title: Nearly Half of NRI Property Owners in India Want to Sell, Survey Finds
excerpt: A Business Standard survey reveals growing NRI disenchantment with Indian real estate as tax changes, low rental yields, and overseas alternatives drive a sell-off sentiment.
body:
• A new Business Standard survey finds 46% of NRI property owners in India want to sell their holdings, with 26% planning exits within six months.
  • Recent tax changes, including removal of indexation benefits and a flat 12.5% LTCG rate, have increased the effective tax burden on long-held NRI properties.
  • Budget 2026 eased one friction point by letting residential buyers skip the TAN requirement when purchasing from NRI sellers.
  • Low rental yields of 2-3% in Indian residential real estate continue to push NRIs toward alternative investments like REITs, mutual funds, and Dubai property.

Nearly half of all NRI property owners in India are now looking to sell, according to a survey reported by Business Standard, in what marks a significant shift in diaspora sentiment toward Indian real estate.

The survey found that 46% of NRI property owners want to exit their Indian holdings, with 26% planning to sell within the next six months. The urgency reflects a convergence of unfavorable tax changes, persistently low rental returns, and growing competition from overseas markets like Dubai and London.

Tax Changes Are Driving the Exodus

The most significant catalyst has been the 2024 overhaul of India's capital gains tax regime. The removal of indexation benefits, which previously allowed property sellers to adjust their purchase price for inflation, has hit NRIs particularly hard. Under the new flat 12.5% long-term capital gains rate, sellers of properties held for decades face substantially higher tax bills than under the old indexed system.

Consider a property purchased for Rs 50 lakh in 2005 and sold today for Rs 2 crore. Under the old regime with indexation, the tax liability might have been around Rs 15 lakh. Under the new 12.5% flat rate without indexation, the same sale now triggers roughly Rs 18.75 lakh in tax, despite the seemingly lower percentage.

"The removal of the indexation benefit is likely to dampen NRI enthusiasm for Indian real estate."

— Mumbai-based tax consultant, as reported by VisaVerge

Adding to the complexity, NRI sellers face a steep 20% TDS deduction on the full sale price, not just the capital gain. While this amount is refundable through the income tax return process, it locks up significant working capital for 12 to 18 months. On a Rs 2 crore sale, that means Rs 40 lakh held by the tax department before any refund materializes.

Budget 2026 Offers Limited Relief

The Union Budget 2026 attempted to address one persistent friction point in NRI property transactions. Previously, any Indian resident buying property from an NRI seller was required to obtain a Tax Deduction and Collection Account Number, or TAN, even for a single transaction. This requirement frequently delayed deals and deterred potential buyers.

Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman announced that TDS on NRI property sales can now be deducted and deposited using the buyer's PAN-based challan, eliminating the TAN requirement. The change takes effect from October 1, 2026.

While the simplification is welcome, market participants say it does little to address the fundamental tax burden driving NRIs toward the exit.

The Rental Yield Problem

Beyond tax concerns, Indian residential property continues to deliver poor income returns. Gross rental yields in major cities average just 2-3%, according to ANAROCK Research. A Rs 80 lakh apartment in Pune or Bengaluru typically rents for Rs 15,000 to Rs 20,000 per month, translating to an annual gross yield of barely 2.5%.

Compare this to Indian government bond yields above 7%, or Dubai's net rental income of 5-9%, and the calculus becomes clear. When combined with total transaction costs of 12-15% for a round-trip purchase and sale, Indian residential property is increasingly difficult to justify as an investment for absentee owners.

Looking Abroad

The sell-off sentiment coincides with growing NRI interest in overseas markets. Dubai's tax-free environment, Golden Visa program, and 100% foreign ownership rights are drawing substantial Indian capital, particularly after recent price corrections made select properties available at 12-15% discounts.

CBRE's India Residential Market Outlook 2026 notes that while the high-end segment continues to attract NRI buyers driven by emotional attachment and family needs, the investment case has weakened considerably. The flight-to-quality trend means NRIs who do buy are concentrating on premium branded residences from established developers rather than speculative purchases.

What NRIs Should Consider

For NRIs contemplating a sale, timing and tax planning are critical. Applying for a Lower TDS Certificate through Form 13 before the sale can prevent excessive upfront deduction. Properties acquired before 2001 may benefit from a Fair Market Value assessment that establishes a higher cost basis, legally reducing the capital gains liability.

The broader trend, however, appears clear: a generation of NRIs who bought Indian property as an emotional anchor to home are now running the numbers and finding them wanting.
nri_angle: Directly affects millions of NRIs who own property in India and are reassessing their holdings amid unfavorable tax changes and low yields.
author: Diaspora Desk
